absent: Allocation, reference counting and teardown rules for kernfs nodes, roots and namespace tags beyond the references shown in link creation and tree setup.
Lock ordering between kernfs semaphores, inode semaphores, dentry locks and the global superblock lock.
Contents and contracts of kernfs extended attribute handlers, export operations, permission and attribute operations referenced only by table membership.
Implementation and error behavior of ancestor search, dcache lookup, slow lookup and common permission bypassing lookup helpers.
Semantics of the shared recursive removal implementation including its exclusive mode and callback invocation guarantees.
Generation, uniqueness and persistence meaning of the random superblock identifier.
Maple tree allocation, reverse search and concurrency guarantees underlying the offset context tree.
Superblock shrinker, passive reference and device table lifecycle outside the insertion and registration fragments shown.

findings.text: Resolves a kernfs node to a referenced dentry inside a kernfs superblock, returning the superblock root directly for the root node and otherwise walking ancestors with permission bypassing positive lookups, requiring roots that guarantee stable parents and reporting invalid input, missing ancestors or allocation shortage as failures.

Provides name resolution that bypasses permission checks and guarantees a positive result, turning cached negative outcomes into a missing entry failure while propagating underlying lookup errors and falling back from cache to slow resolution when needed.

Completes initialization of a new kernfs superblock by recording its private info, applying restrictive execution and device behavior, page sized block geometry, caller supplied filesystem identity, kernfs operation vectors and attribute handlers with conditional export support, fine timestamp granularity and large file limits, then attaching a root inode and root dentry with default dentry behavior.
Reuse of an existing kernfs superblock depends only on equality of the filesystem root and of the namespace tag between the incumbent and the incoming context.

Obtains a superblock for a filesystem context through shared lookup with anonymous device assignment, performing full fill, activation, fresh identifier recording and supers list registration only when no root exists yet, and always leaving a referenced root dentry in the context on success.

Insertion and removal of superblock info on the owning root supers collection occur exclusively under the root supers write lock, covering both acquisition of a new superblock and teardown of an existing one.

Superblock teardown detaches its info from the root collection before marking the anonymous instance dead and releasing the info allocation, while filesystem context cleanup releases only the info allocation and explicitly leaves namespace tag ownership to the caller.

Anonymous superblock setup assigns a device number with zero major part and a strictly positive minor part drawn from a bounded pool, mapping pool exhaustion to a file table overflow failure and releasing the number when registration fails.
Device registration for a superblock requires the global superblock lock to be held and verifies that a device value and a registration record are present before attempting table insertion.
Successful recording of a superblock device association increments a passive reference on the owning superblock, while failed recording clears the stored device value to avoid a dangling association.

Symlink creation inherits ownership from target attribute overrides when present and otherwise uses root ownership, creates a world accessible link node, propagates namespace when the parent family requires it, stores the target with an owning reference, and releases the new node when final insertion fails.

Relative target text for a symlink is limited to the system maximum path length, rejects overlong construction and degenerate empty results, and is formed by ascending to a shared ancestor with parent prefix segments followed by reverse filling of the descendant remainder.

Reading a link fills a caller visible page sized buffer from the stored target node while holding the filesystem read lock, transferring buffer ownership to the completion callback on success and reporting allocation or path construction problems as failures.
Symlink inodes publish a fixed operation set covering extended attribute listing, link reading, attribute update and query, and permission checking, all drawn from the kernfs inode operation family.

Simple in memory directories provide two file operation families, one cursor based with open close seek directory read iteration and synchronization, and one offset map based with seek shared iteration directory read synchronization and lease management, plus a minimal inode operation set that handles lookup only.

Lookup in simple filesystems rejects overlong names, disables caching for plain dentries that carry no operations, delegates case folded directories back to the caller for further handling, and otherwise resolves through alias splicing without instantiating new inodes.
The unconditional dentry removal helper always requests deletion, so any user of it must expect the dentry to be discarded rather than retained.
Attribute reporting for simple inodes uses generic filling under the neutral identity mapping and derives block consumption from the number of cached pages expressed in standard units.

Cursor based directory scanning serializes sibling walks with the parent dentry lock, stabilizes positive candidates with nested child locks and double checking, skips cursor entries to prevent livelock, and may temporarily release the parent lock around scheduling while remembering its position.

Cursor directory file positions zero and one correspond to the dot entries, with higher positions mapping to successive positive siblings; seeks accept absolute and relative forms only for nonnegative results and reposition or detach the cursor accordingly while updating the recorded position.

The first usable directory position for real entries is two and the end of directory marker is the largest signed thirty two bit value, with dynamically assigned offsets constrained strictly inside that interval.

Offset tracking stores a numeric cookie in per dentry private data backed by a range allocating tree, refusing entries that already carry a cookie, converting allocation contention into a no space failure, and clearing both tree and cookie on removal with full tree release on context destruction.

Rename handling moves or exchanges stored offset cookies through the old and new directory contexts, warning and abandoning the transfer when required cookies are missing and restoring the prior mapping when the second store of an exchange fails, while also adjusting directory link counts for cross directory moves involving directories and refreshing modification and change times on all participants.

Offset based directory iteration requires the directory inode semaphore held for reading, performs map based ancestor searches under read side protection, and selects candidate siblings under parent and nested child dentry locks with double checking of positivity.

Offset iteration always emits dot entries first, resolves the starting sibling from the current position through map lookup or from the beginning for the first entry, advances by stored cookies while emitting each entry, and parks the position at the end marker when no further positive sibling exists.
Opening a cursor based directory allocates a cursor entry owned by the open file and reports memory shortage on failure, while closing drops the cursor reference and unconditionally reports success.

Removal by name resolves the child through a permission bypassing positive only lookup and only on success recursively removes that subtree and drops the lookup reference, with the recursive helper delegating to shared logic in nonexclusive mode.

Reading of kernfs names, parent relationships, symlink targets and root inode instantiation is confined to sections protected by the filesystem read lock, including ancestor selection and link path construction.

Attempting node to dentry resolution on a root that does not guarantee stable parents, or encountering a missing ancestor during the walk, is treated as a programming error and fails as invalid input instead of using an unstable chain.
Link reading without a dentry context fails as an invalid child resolution request rather than proceeding, ensuring that speculative child lookups do not dereference absent state.
Kernfs superblocks use machine page size for block size with its matching shift, advertise the largest regular file size and unit timestamp granularity, and prohibit execution and device nodes.
Recording a superblock identifier truncates inputs longer than available storage with a warning and persists the effective length alongside the copied bytes.
Each offset context initializes its map for range allocation under a dedicated lock class and seeds the next allocation cursor just above the first real directory entry.
Cursor seeking holds the directory inode in shared mode while locating the destination sibling and mutates cursor linkage only while holding the parent dentry lock.
Whether an inode participates in case insensitive handling is decided by a single flag bit in its persistent inode flags.
The namespace associated with a kernfs superblock is obtained directly from its private info without locking or reference transfer.

Offset directory seeking accepts absolute and relative forms, rejects negative results and unknown modes as invalid, and otherwise delegates final positioning to the common file position helper with a wide upper bound.
Ordinary read requests against simple directory file descriptions always fail as inappropriate directory access rather than returning directory data.
